caption:
Was the Cardiff Giant real? No — and the man who made it wanted you to find out.

In 1868 New York tobacconist George Hull lost an argument at a Methodist revival about Genesis 6:4, the verse saying giants once lived on Earth. Angry at how easily people believed, he decided to build one.

With H. B. Martin he had a block of gypsum 10 feet 4½ inches long quarried at Fort Dodge, Iowa, telling the workmen it was for a Lincoln monument. It went to Chicago, where sculptors Henry Salle and Fred Mohrmann carved it behind hung quilts to muffle the sound. The surface was beaten with steel knitting needles set in a board to fake pores, then washed with sand and sulphuric acid. The face was modelled on Hull himself. A geologist told him hair would not petrify, so the giant has none.

It was buried on his cousin William Newell's farm in November 1868. Almost a year later, on 16 October 1869, men Newell had hired to dig a well found it. Newell charged fifty cents for a fifteen-minute look and drew three to five hundred people a day.

Geologists broke it fast. Yale's Othniel C. Marsh called it "a most decided humbug" — soluble gypsum buried for centuries would not still carry fresh tool marks. Cornell's Andrew D. White noted there was no reason to dig a well in that spot at all. Hull confessed on 10 December 1869; on 2 February 1870 a court declared both his giant and P. T. Barnum's plaster copy fakes.

Still unresolved: whether Edward Burkhardt, the Chicago stonecutter who took the block, knew what he was helping to make. The record does not say.

Images: an 1869 lithograph of "The Onondaga Giant"; a Bain News Service negative of the giant, 1910; and both sides of an 1873 stereocard of Cardiff Glen, Iowa, from the New York Public Library.
